rationale: This qualitative empirical study (interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists in Khayelitsha, Cape Town) examines household/community sanitation access (open toilets, bucket disposal, inadequate service provision) and identifies a concrete legal/administrative mechanism—municipal authorities' continued classification of the informal settlement as 'temporary'—that perpetuates inadequate sanitation service provision and conditional exclusion. All eligibility criteria (C1–C4) are clearly met.
plain_vs_narrow_note: Both the plain and narrow Criterion 2 readings support inclusion because the study examines a specific administrative/tenure classification mechanism—official classification of the informal settlement as 'temporary'—that directly restricts municipal sanitation service provision.

evidence_quotes.quote: Although authorities acknowledge the crisis, the continued classification of the settlement as “temporary” perpetuates inadequate service provision and entrenches vulnerability.
Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists, supported by computer-assisted coding in ATLAS. ti 22
Testimonies reveal how inadequate sanitation systems, including open toilets, bucket disposal, and stagnant wastewater, exacerbate illness and psychosocial stress in densely packed dwellings.
